{{Short description|Graph layout on multiple half-planes}}

{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
[[File:3page K5.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|A three-page book embedding of the [[complete graph]] {{math|''K''<sub>5</sub>}}. Because it is not a [[planar graph]], it is not possible to embed this graph without crossings on fewer pages, so its book thickness is three.|alt=Refer to caption]]
In [[graph theory]], a '''book embedding''' is a generalization of [[planar graph|planar embedding]] of a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] to embeddings in a ''book'', a collection of [[half-plane]]s all having the same [[Line (geometry)|line]] as their boundary. Usually, the vertices of the graph are required to lie on this boundary line, called the ''spine'', and the edges are required to stay within a single half-plane. The '''book thickness''' of a graph is the smallest possible number of half-planes for any book embedding of the graph. Book thickness is also called '''pagenumber''', '''stacknumber''' or '''fixed outerthickness'''. Book embeddings have also been used to define several other [[graph invariant]]s including the pagewidth and book crossing number.

Every graph with {{mvar|n}} vertices has book thickness at most <math>\lceil n/2\rceil</math>, and this formula gives the exact book thickness for [[complete graph]]s. The graphs with book thickness one are the [[outerplanar graph]]s. The graphs with book thickness at most two are the [[subhamiltonian graph]]s, which are always [[planar graph|planar]]; more generally, every planar graph has book thickness at most four. It is [[NP-hard]] to determine the exact book thickness of a given graph, with or without knowing a fixed vertex ordering along the spine of the book. Testing the existence of a three-page book embedding of a graph, given a fixed ordering of the vertices along the spine of the embedding, has unknown computational complexity: it is neither known to be solvable in polynomial time nor known to be NP-hard.

One of the original motivations for studying book embeddings involved applications in [[VLSI]] design, in which the vertices of a book embedding represent components of a circuit and the wires represent connections between them. Book embedding also has applications in [[graph drawing]], where two of the standard visualization styles for graphs, [[arc diagram]]s and [[circular layout]]s, can be constructed using book embeddings.

In [[transportation planning]], the different sources and destinations of foot and vehicle traffic that meet and interact at a [[traffic light]] can be modeled mathematically as the vertices of a graph, with edges connecting different source-destination pairs. A book embedding of this graph can be used to design a schedule that lets all the traffic move across the intersection with as few signal phases as possible. In [[bioinformatics]] problems involving the folding structure of [[RNA]], single-page book embeddings represent classical forms of [[nucleic acid secondary structure]], and two-page book embeddings represent [[pseudoknot]]s. Other applications of book embeddings include  [[abstract algebra]] and [[knot theory]].

==History==
The notion of a book, as a topological space, was defined by C. A. Persinger and Gail Atneosen in the 1960s.<ref name="persinger"/><ref name="a68">{{citation
 | last = Atneosen | first = Gail Adele
 | series = Ph.D. thesis
 | mr = 2617705
 | page = 79
 | publisher = [[Michigan State University]]
 | title = On the embeddability of compacta in <math>n</math>-books: intrinsic and extrinsic properties
 | url = http://gateway.proquest.com/openurl?url_ver=Z39.88-2004&rft_val_fmt=info:ofi/fmt:kev:mtx:dissertation&res_dat=xri:pqdiss&rft_dat=xri:pqdiss:6905835
 | year = 1968}}. See also {{citation
 | last = Atneosen | first = Gail H.
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Fundamenta Mathematicae]]
 | mr = 0293592
 | pages = 43–45
 | title = One-dimensional <math>n</math>-leaved continua
 | url = http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/fm/fm74/fm7415.pdf
 | volume = 74
 | year = 1972
 | doi=10.4064/fm-74-1-43-45| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> As part of this work, Atneosen already considered embeddings of graphs in books. The embeddings he studied used the same definition as embeddings of graphs into any other topological space: vertices are represented by distinct points, edges are represented by curves, and the only way that two edges can intersect is for them to meet at a common endpoint.

In the early 1970s,  [[Paul Chester Kainen|Paul C. Kainen]] and L. Taylor Ollmann developed a more restricted type of embedding that came to be used in most subsequent research. In their formulation, the graph's vertices must be placed along the spine of the book, and each edge must lie in a single page.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Kainen | first = Paul C. | authorlink = Paul Chester Kainen
 | editor1-last = Bari | editor1-first = Ruth A.
 | editor2-last = Harary | editor2-first = Frank | editor2-link = Frank Harary
 | contribution = Some recent results in topological graph theory
 | pages = 76–108
 | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics
 | title = Graphs and Combinatorics (Proceedings of the Capital Conference on Graph Theory and Combinatorics at the George Washington University June 18–22, 1973)
 | volume = 406
 | year = 1974}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Ollmann | first = L. Taylor
 | editor1-last = Hoffman | editor1-first = Frederick
 | editor2-last = Levow | editor2-first = Roy B.
 | editor3-last = Thomas | editor3-first = Robert S. D.
 | contribution = On the book thicknesses of various graphs
 | page = 459
 | series = Congressus Numerantium
 | title = Proc. 4th Southeastern Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory and Computing
 | volume = VIII
 | year = 1973}}.</ref>
Important milestones in the later development of book embeddings include the proof by [[Mihalis Yannakakis]] in the late 1980s that [[planar graphs]] have book thickness at most four,<ref name="yan89"/><ref name="yan86"/> and the discovery in the late 1990s of close connections between book embeddings and [[bioinformatics]].<ref name="hs99"/>

==Definitions==
[[File:K3,3 2-page 1-crossing.svg|thumb|The [[utility graph]] ''K''<sub>3,3</sub> has no 2-page book embedding, but it can be drawn as shown in a 2-page book with only one crossing. Therefore, its 2-page book crossing number is 1.|alt=Refer to caption]]
[[File:Diamond pagewidth.svg|thumb|upright=0.85|This 1-page embedding of the [[diamond graph]] has pagewidth&nbsp;3, because the yellow ray crosses three edges.|alt=Refer to caption]]
A '''book''' is a particular kind of [[topological space]], also called a [[Sheaf of planes|fan]] of half-planes.<ref name="persinger">{{citation
 | last = Persinger | first = C. A.
 | doi = 10.2140/pjm.1966.18.169
 | journal = [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]]
 | mr = 0195077
 | pages = 169–173
 | title = Subsets of <math>n</math>-books in <math>E^3</math>
 | volume = 18
 | year = 1966| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref name="hales">{{citation
 | last = Hales | first = T. C. | authorlink = Thomas Callister Hales
 | doi = 10.1007/PL00009312
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Discrete and Computational Geometry]]
 | mr = 1455511
 | pages = 135–149
 | title = Sphere packings. II
 | volume = 18
 | year = 1997| doi-access = free
 | hdl = 2027.42/42419
 | hdl-access = free
 }}.</ref> It consists of a single [[Line (geometry)|line]] {{mvar|ℓ}}, called the '''spine''' or '''back''' of the book, together with a collection of one or more [[half-plane]]s, called the '''pages''' or '''leaves''' of the book,<ref>The "spine" and "pages" terminology is more standard in modern graph-theoretic approaches to the subject. For the "back" and "leaves" terminology, see {{harvtxt|Persinger|1966}}.</ref> each having the spine as its boundary. Books with a [[finite set|finite number]] of pages can be [[Embedding|embedded]] into [[three-dimensional space]], for instance by choosing {{mvar|ℓ}} to be the {{mvar|z}}-axis of a [[Cartesian coordinate system]] and choosing the pages to be the {{mvar|k}} half-planes whose [[dihedral angle]] with respect to the {{mvar|xz}}-plane is an integer multiple of {{math|2{{pi}}/''k''}}.<ref name="bk"/>

A '''book drawing''' of a finite graph {{mvar|G}} onto a book {{mvar|B}} is a [[graph drawing|drawing]] of {{mvar|G}} on {{mvar|B}} such that every vertex of {{mvar|G}} is drawn as a point on the spine of {{mvar|B}}, and every edge of {{mvar|G}} is drawn as a [[curve]] that lies within a single page of {{mvar|B}}. The {{mvar|k}}-page '''book crossing number''' of {{mvar|G}} is the minimum [[crossing number (graph theory)|number of crossings]] in a {{mvar|k}}-page book drawing.<ref name="sssv">{{citation
 | last1 = Shahrokhi | first1 = Farhad
 | last2 = Székely | first2 = László A.
 | last3 = Sýkora | first3 = Ondrej
 | last4 = Vrťo | first4 = Imrich
 | doi = 10.1002/(SICI)1097-0118(199604)21:4<413::AID-JGT7>3.3.CO;2-5
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Journal of Graph Theory]]
 | mr = 1377615
 | pages = 413–424
 | title = The book crossing number of a graph
 | volume = 21
 | year = 1996}}.</ref>

A '''book embedding''' of {{mvar|G}} onto {{mvar|B}} is a book drawing that forms a [[graph embedding]] of {{mvar|G}} into {{mvar|B}}. That is, it is a book drawing of {{mvar|G}} on {{mvar|B}} that does not have any edge crossings.
Every finite graph has a book embedding onto a book with a large enough number of pages. For instance, it is always possible to embed each edge of the graph on its own separate page.
The '''book thickness''', '''pagenumber''', or '''stack number''' of {{mvar|G}} is the minimum number of pages required for a book embedding of&nbsp;{{mvar|G}}.
Another parameter that measures the quality of a book embedding, beyond its number of pages, is its '''pagewidth'''. This is defined analogously to [[cutwidth]] as the maximum number of edges that can be crossed by a [[ray (geometry)|ray]] perpendicular to the spine within a single page. Equivalently (for book embeddings in which each edge is drawn as a monotonic curve), it is the maximum size of a subset of edges within a single page such that the [[interval (mathematics)|intervals]] defined on the spine by pairs of endpoints of the edges all intersect each other.<ref name="h87"/><ref>{{citation
 | last = Stöhr | first = Elena
 | doi = 10.1016/0890-5401(88)90036-3
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Information and Computation]]
 | mr = 968104
 | pages = 155–162
 | title = A trade-off between page number and page width of book embeddings of graphs
 | volume = 79
 | year = 1988| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Stöhr | first = Elena
 | doi = 10.1016/0012-365X(91)90398-L
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1108073
 | pages = 43–49
 | title = The pagewidth of trivalent planar graphs
 | volume = 89
 | year = 1991| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

It is crucial for these definitions that edges are only allowed to stay within a single page of the book. As Atneosen already observed, if edges may instead pass from one page to another across the spine of the book, then every graph may be embedded into a three-page book.<ref name="em99"/><ref name="a68"/><ref name="bo99"/> For such a three-page '''topological book embedding''' in which spine crossings are allowed, every graph can be embedded with at most a logarithmic number of spine crossings per edge,<ref name="em99">{{citation
 | last1 = Enomoto | first1 = Hikoe
 | last2 = Miyauchi | first2 = Miki Shimabara
 | doi = 10.1137/S0895480195280319
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1710241
 | pages = 337–341
 | title = Embedding graphs into a three page book with <math>O(M\log N)</math> crossings of edges over the spine
 | volume = 12
 | year = 1999}}.</ref> and some graphs need this many spine crossings.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Enomoto | first1 = Hikoe
 | last2 = Miyauchi | first2 = Miki Shimabara
 | last3 = Ota | first3 = Katsuhiro
 | doi = 10.1016/S0166-218X(99)00044-X
 | issue = 2–3
 | journal = [[Discrete Applied Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1697548
 | pages = 149–155
 | title = Lower bounds for the number of edge-crossings over the spine in a topological book embedding of a graph
 | volume = 92
 | year = 1999| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

==Specific graphs==
As shown in the first figure, the book thickness of the [[complete graph]] {{math|''K''<sub>5</sub>}} is three: as a non-planar graph its book thickness is greater than two, but a book embedding with three pages exists. More generally, the book thickness of every complete graph with {{math|''n'' ≥ 4}} vertices is exactly <math>\lceil n/2\rceil</math>. This result also gives an [[upper bound]] on the maximum possible book thickness of any {{mvar|n}}-vertex graph.<ref name="bk"/>

The two-page crossing number of the complete graph {{math|''K''<sub>''n''</sub>}} is
:<math>\frac{1}{4} \biggl\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\biggr\rfloor\biggl\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\biggr\rfloor\biggl\lfloor\frac{n-2}{2}\biggr\rfloor\biggl\lfloor\frac{n-3}{2}\biggr\rfloor,</math>
matching a still-unproven conjecture of [[Anthony Hill (artist)|Anthony Hill]] on what the unrestricted crossing number of this graph should be. That is, if Hill's conjecture is correct, then the drawing of this graph that minimizes the number of crossings is a two-page drawing.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ábrego | first1 = Bernardo M.
 | last2 = Aichholzer | first2 = Oswin
 | last3 = Fernández-Merchant | first3 = Silvia
 | last4 = Ramos | first4 = Pedro
 | last5 = Salazar | first5 = Gelasio
 | contribution = The 2-page crossing number of <math>K_n</math> (extended abstract)
 | doi = 10.1145/2261250.2261310
 | mr = 3050657
 | pages = 397–403
 | publisher = ACM, New York
 | title = Proceedings of the 28th Annual Symposium on Computational Geometry (SCG'12)
 | year = 2012
 }}.</ref>

The book thickness of the [[complete bipartite graph]] {{math|''K''<sub>''a'',''b''</sub>}} is at most {{math|min(''a'',''b'')}}. To construct a drawing with this book thickness, for each vertex on the smaller side of the bipartition, one can place the edges incident with that vertex on their own page. This bound is not always tight; for instance, {{math|''K''<sub>4,4</sub>}} has book thickness three, not four. However, when the two sides of the graph are very unbalanced, with {{math|''b'' > ''a''(''a'' &minus; 1)}}, the book thickness of {{math|''K''<sub>''a'',''b''</sub>}} is exactly {{mvar|a}}.<ref name="bk"/><ref>For additional results on the book thickness of complete bipartite graphs, see {{citation
 | last1 = Enomoto | first1 = Hikoe
 | last2 = Nakamigawa | first2 = Tomoki
 | last3 = Ota | first3 = Katsuhiro
 | doi = 10.1006/jctb.1997.1773
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]
 | mr = 1469870
 | pages = 111–120
 | series = Series B
 | title = On the pagenumber of complete bipartite graphs
 | volume = 71
 | year = 1997| doi-access = free
 }}; {{citation
 | last1 = de Klerk | first1 = Etienne
 | last2 = Pasechnik | first2 = Dmitrii V.
 | last3 = Salazar | first3 = Gelasio
 | doi = 10.1016/j.dam.2013.11.001
 | journal = [[Discrete Applied Mathematics]]
 | mr = 3166108
 | pages = 80–93
 | title = Book drawings of complete bipartite graphs
 | volume = 167
 | year = 2014| arxiv = 1210.2918
 }}.</ref>

For the [[Turán graph]] {{math|''T''(''kr'',''r'')}} (a [[complete multipartite graph]] {{math|''K''<sub>''k'',''k'',...</sub>}} formed from {{mvar|r}} [[independent set (graph theory)|independent sets]] of {{mvar|k}} vertices per independent set, with an edge between every two vertices from different independent sets) the book thickness {{mvar|t}} is sandwiched between
:<math>\left\lceil \frac{k(r-1)}{2}\right\rceil \le t \le \left\lceil \frac{kr}{2} \right\rceil</math>
and when {{mvar|r}} is odd the upper bound can be improved to
:<math>t\le (r-1)\left\lceil\frac{k}{2}\right\rceil + \left\lceil \frac{k}{4} \right\rceil.</math><ref name="bk"/><ref>{{citation

==Properties==

===Planarity and outerplanarity===
[[File:Goldner-Harary graph.svg|thumb|The [[Goldner–Harary graph]], a planar graph with book thickness three|alt=Refer to caption]]
The book thickness of a given graph {{mvar|G}} is at most one if and only if {{mvar|G}} is an [[outerplanar graph]]. An outerplanar graph is a graph that has a planar embedding in which all vertices belong to the outer face of the embedding. For such a graph, placing the vertices in the same order along the spine as they appear in the outer face provides a one-page book embedding of the given graph. (An [[articulation point]] of the graph will necessarily appear more than once in the cyclic ordering of vertices around the outer face, but only one of those copies should be included in the book embedding.) Conversely, a one-page book embedding is automatically an outerplanar embedding. For, if a graph is embedded on a single page, and another half-plane is attached to the spine to extend its page to a complete plane, then the outer face of the embedding includes the entire added half-plane, and all vertices lie on this outer face.<ref name="bk"/><ref name="h87"/>

Every two-page book embedding is a special case of a planar embedding, because the union of two pages of a book is a space topologically equivalent to the whole plane. Therefore, every graph with book thickness two is automatically a [[planar graph]]. More precisely, the book thickness of a graph {{mvar|G}} is at most two if and only if {{mvar|G}} is a [[Glossary of graph theory#Subgraphs|subgraph]] of a planar graph that has a [[Hamiltonian cycle]].<ref name="bk">{{citation
 | last1 = Bernhart | first1 = Frank R.
 | last2 = Kainen | first2 = Paul C. | author2-link = Paul Chester Kainen
 | doi = 10.1016/0095-8956(79)90021-2
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]
 | mr = 0554297
 | pages = 320–331
 | series = Series B
 | title = The book thickness of a graph
 | volume = 27
 | year = 1979| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> If a graph is given a two-page embedding, it can be augmented to a planar Hamiltonian graph by adding (into any page) extra edges between any two consecutive vertices along the spine that are not already adjacent, and between the first and last spine vertices. The [[Goldner–Harary graph]] provides an example of a planar graph that does not have book thickness two: it is a [[maximal planar graph]], so it is not possible to add any edges to it while preserving planarity, and it does not have a Hamiltonian cycle.<ref name="bk"/> Because of this characterization by Hamiltonian cycles, graphs that have two-page book embeddings are also known as [[subhamiltonian graph]]s.<ref name="h87">{{citation
 | last = Heath | first = Lenwood S.
 | doi = 10.1137/0608018
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods]]
 | mr = 881181
 | pages = 198–218
 | title = Embedding outerplanar graphs in small books
 | volume = 8
 | year = 1987}}.</ref>

All planar graphs whose [[degree (graph theory)|maximum degree]] is at most four have book thickness at most two.<ref name="bgr14">{{citation
 | last1 = Bekos | first1 = Michael A.
 | last2 = Gronemann | first2 = Martin
 | last3 = Raftopoulou | first3 = Chrysanthi N.
 | arxiv = 1401.0684
 | contribution = Two-page book embeddings of 4-planar graphs
 | doi = 10.4230/LIPIcs.STACS.2014.137
 | pages = 137–148
 | title = Proceedings of the 31st Symposium on Theoretical Aspects of Computer Science
 | year = 2014| title-link = Symposium on Theoretical Aspects of Computer Science
 | series = Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs)
 | volume = 25
 | doi-access = free
 | isbn = 9783939897651
 }}.</ref> [[Apollonian network|Planar 3-trees]] have book thickness at most three.<ref name="hea84">{{citation
 | last1 = Heath | first1 = Lenny
 | contribution = Embedding planar graphs In seven pages
 | doi = 10.1109/SFCS.1984.715903
 | pages = 74–83
 | title = Proceedings of the 25th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science
 | year = 1984| title-link = Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science
 | isbn = 0-8186-0591-X
 }}.</ref> More generally, all planar graphs have book thickness four.<ref name="yan89"/><ref name="yan86"/><ref name="bkk2020"/> It has been claimed by [[Mihalis Yannakakis]] in 1986<ref name="yan86">{{citation|contribution=Four pages are necessary and sufficient for planar graphs|first=Mihalis|last=Yannakakis|authorlink=Mihalis Yannakakis|title=Proceedings of the 18th ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC '86)|year=1986|pages=104–108|doi=10.1145/12130.12141|isbn=0-89791-193-8|title-link=Symposium on Theory of Computing}}.</ref> that there exist some planar graphs that have book thickness exactly four. However, a detailed proof of this claim, announced in a subsequent journal paper,<ref name="yan89">{{citation|title=Embedding planar graphs in four pages|first=Mihalis|last=Yannakakis|authorlink=Mihalis Yannakakis|journal=[[Journal of Computer and System Sciences]]|volume=38|year=1989|pages=36–67|doi=10.1016/0022-0000(89)90032-9|doi-access=free}}</ref> was not known until 2020, when Bekos et al.<ref name="bkk2020">{{citation
 | last1 = Bekos | first1 = Michael A.
 | last2 = Kaufmann | first2 = Micheal
 | last3 = Klute | first3 = Fabian
 | last4 = Pupyrev | first4 = Sergey
 | last5 = Raftopoulou | first5 = Chrysanthi
 | last6 = Ueckerdt | first6 = Torsten
 | arxiv = 2004.07630
 | title = Four Pages Are Indeed Necessary for Planar Graphs
 | issue = 11
 | volume = 1
 | journal =  Journal of Computational Geomerty
 | pages = 332–353 
 | year = 2020}}.</ref> presented planar graphs with [[treewidth]] 4 that require four pages in any book embedding.

===Behavior under subdivisions===
[[File:Diamond graph.svg|thumb|upright=0.75|The book thickness of the diamond graph increases after edge subdivision|alt=Refer to caption]]
[[Homeomorphism (graph theory)|Subdividing]] every edge of a graph into two-edge paths, by adding new vertices within each edge, may sometimes increase its book thickness. For instance, the [[diamond graph]] has book thickness one (it is outerplanar) but its subdivision has book thickness two (it is planar and subhamiltonian but not outerplanar). However, this subdivision process can also sometimes significantly reduce the book thickness of the subdivided graph. For instance, the book thickness of the [[complete graph]] {{math|''K''<sub>''n''</sub>}} is proportional to its number of vertices, but subdividing each of its edges into a two-edge path produces a subdivision whose book thickness is much smaller, only <math>O(\sqrt n)</math>.<ref name="e01">{{cite arXiv|title=Separating geometric thickness from book thickness|first=David|last=Eppstein|authorlink=David Eppstein|eprint=math.CO/0109195|year=2001|mode=cs2}}.</ref> Despite the existence of examples such as this one, {{harvtxt|Blankenship|Oporowski|1999}} [[conjecture]]d that a subdivision's book thickness cannot be too much smaller than that of the original graph. Specifically, they conjectured that there exists a function {{mvar|f}} such that, for every graph {{mvar|G}} and for the graph {{mvar|H}} formed by replacing every edge in {{mvar|G}} by a two-edge path, if the book thickness of {{mvar|H}} is {{mvar|t}} then the book thickness of {{mvar|G}} is at most {{math|''f''(''t'')}}.<ref name="bo99">{{citation|first1=Robin|last1=Blankenship|first2=Bogdan|last2=Oporowski|title=Drawing Subdivisions Of Complete And Complete Bipartite Graphs On Books|series=Technical Report 1999-4|publisher=Department of Mathematics, Louisiana State University|year=1999}}.</ref> Their conjecture turned out to be false: graphs formed by [[Cartesian product of graphs|Cartesian products]] of [[star (graph theory)|stars]] and [[triangular tiling]]s have unbounded book thickness, but subdividing their edges into six-edge paths reduces their book thickness to three.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Dujmović | first1 = Vida | author1-link = Vida Dujmović
 | last2 = Eppstein | first2 = David | author2-link = David Eppstein
 | last3 = Hickingbotham | first3 = Robert
 | last4 = Morin | first4 = Pat | author4-link = Pat Morin
 | last5 = Wood | first5 = David R. | author5-link = David Wood (mathematician)
 | arxiv = 2011.04195
 | date = August 2021
 | doi = 10.1007/s00493-021-4585-7
 | journal = [[Combinatorica]]
 | title = Stack-number is not bounded by queue-number| volume = 42 | issue = 2 | pages = 151–164 }}</ref>

===Relation to other graph invariants===
Book thickness is related to [[thickness (graph theory)|thickness]], the number of planar graphs needed to cover the edges of the given graph. A graph {{mvar|G}} has thickness {{mvar|&theta;}} if it can be drawn in the plane, and its edges [[edge coloring|colored]] with {{mvar|&theta;}} colors, in such a way that edges of the same color as each other do not cross. Analogously, a graph {{mvar|G}} has book thickness {{mvar|&theta;}} if it can be drawn in a [[half plane]], with its vertices on the boundary of the half plane, with its edges colored with {{mvar|&theta;}} colors with no crossing between two edges of the same color. In this formulation of book thickness, the colors of the edges correspond to the pages of the book embedding. However, thickness and book thickness can be very different from each other: there exist graphs ([[Homeomorphism (graph theory)|subdivisions]] of [[complete graph]]s) that have unbounded book thickness,<ref name="e01"/><ref name="em99"/><ref name="bo99"/> despite having thickness two.<ref name="e01"/>

Graphs of [[treewidth]] {{mvar|k}} have book thickness at most {{math|''k'' + 1}}<ref name="dw07">{{citation|first1=Vida|last1=Dujmović|author1-link=Vida Dujmović|first2=David R.|last2=Wood|author2-link=David Wood (mathematician)|title=Graph treewidth and geometric thickness parameters|journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]]|volume=37|issue=4|year=2007|pages=641–670|doi=10.1007/s00454-007-1318-7|arxiv=math/0503553}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ganley | first1 = Joseph L.
 | last2 = Heath | first2 = Lenwood S.
 | doi = 10.1016/S0166-218X(00)00178-5
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Discrete Applied Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1818238
 | pages = 215–221
 | title = The pagenumber of <math>k</math>-trees is <math>O(k)</math>
 | volume = 109
 | year = 2001| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> and this bound is tight for 
{{math|''k'' > 2}}.<ref name="dw07"/> Graphs  with {{mvar|m}} edges have book thickness <math>O(\sqrt m)</math>,<ref>{{citation
 | last = Malitz | first = Seth M.
 | doi = 10.1006/jagm.1994.1027
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Journal of Algorithms
 | mr = 1279269
 | pages = 71–84
 | title = Graphs with <math>E</math> edges have pagenumber <math>O(\sqrt{E})</math>
 | volume = 17
 | year = 1994}}.</ref> and graphs of [[Genus (mathematics)|genus]] {{mvar|g}} have book thickness <math>O(\sqrt g)</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Malitz | first = Seth M.
 | doi = 10.1006/jagm.1994.1028
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Journal of Algorithms
 | mr = 1279270
 | pages = 85–109
 | title = Genus <math>g</math> graphs have pagenumber <math>O(\sqrt{g})</math>
 | volume = 17
 | year = 1994}}.</ref> More generally, it has been stated that every [[Robertson–Seymour theorem|minor-closed graph family]] has bounded book thickness.<ref name="nodm">{{citation
 | last1 = Nešetřil | first1 = Jaroslav | author1-link = Jaroslav Nešetřil
 | last2 = Ossona de Mendez | first2 = Patrice | author2-link = Patrice Ossona de Mendez
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-27875-4 | isbn = 978-3-642-27874-7
 | mr = 2920058
 | pages = 321–328
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Algorithms and Combinatorics
 | title = Sparsity: Graphs, Structures, and Algorithms
 | volume = 28
 | year = 2012}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|first=R.|last=Blankenship|title=Book Embeddings of Graphs|series=Ph.D. thesis|publisher=Department of Mathematics, Louisiana State University|year=2003}}. As cited by {{harvtxt|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012}}.</ref> However, the proof of this claim rests on a previous claim that graphs embedded on non-orientable surfaces have bounded book thickness, for which a detailed proof has not been supplied.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ozeki | first1 = Kenta
 | last2 = Nakamoto | first2 = Atsuhiro
 | last3 = Nozawa | first3 = Takayuki

 | volume = 33
 | year = 2019}}</ref> The [[1-planar graph]]s, which are not closed under minors,<ref name="nodm"/> have bounded book thickness,<ref>{{citation

 | last2 = Bruckdorfer | first2 = Till
 | last3 = Kaufmann | first3 = Michael
 | last4 = Raftopoulou | first4 = Chrysanthi

 }}.</ref> but some 1-planar graphs including {{math|''K''<sub>2,2,2,2</sub>}} have book thickness at least four.<ref name="bkz15">{{citation|contribution=The book embedding problem from a SAT-solving perspective|first1=Michael|last1=Bekos|first2=Michael|last2=Kaufmann|first3=Christian|last3=Zielke|pages=113–125|title=Proc. 23rd International Symposium on Graph Drawing and Network Visualization (GD 2015)|year=2015}}.</ref>

Every [[shallow minor]] of a graph of bounded book thickness is a [[sparse graph]], whose ratio of edges to vertices is bounded by a constant that depends only on the depth of the minor and on the book thickness. That is, in the terminology of {{harvtxt|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012}}, the graphs of bounded book thickness have [[bounded expansion]].<ref name="nodm"/> However, even the graphs of bounded [[degree (graph theory)|degree]], a much stronger requirement than having bounded expansion, can have unbounded book thickness.<ref>{{citation

 }}.</ref>

Because graphs of book thickness two are planar graphs, they obey the [[planar separator theorem]]: they have separators, subsets of vertices whose removal splits the graph into pieces with at most {{math|2''n''/3}} vertices each, with only <math>O(\sqrt n)</math> vertices in the separator. Here, {{mvar|n}} refers to the number of vertices in the graph. However, there exist graphs of book thickness three that do not have separators of sublinear size.<ref name="dsw15">{{cite arXiv|title=3-Monotone Expanders|first1=Vida|last1=Dujmović|author1-link=Vida Dujmović|first2=Anastasios|last2=Sidiropoulos|first3=David R.|last3=Wood|author3-link=David Wood (mathematician)|eprint=1501.05020|year=2015|class=math.CO |mode=cs2}}, improving an earlier result showing the existence of expanders with constant pagenumber from {{citation

 | last2 = Yehudayoff | first2 = Amir
 | doi = 10.1007/s00039-012-0200-9
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Geometric and Functional Analysis (journal)|Geometric and Functional Analysis]]
 | mr = 3037896
 | pages = 1–41
 | title = Expansion in <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})</math> and monotone expanders
 | volume = 23
 | year = 2013 }}. See also {{citation

 | last3 = Szemerédi | first3 = Endre | author3-link = Endre Szemerédi
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02122679
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Combinatorica]]
 | mr = 1010295

 | title = On 3-pushdown graphs with large separators
 | volume = 9
 | year = 1989 }}; {{citation
 | last1 = Dvir | first1 = Zeev
 | last2 = Wigderson | first2 = Avi | author2-link = Avi Wigderson
 | doi = 10.4086/toc.2010.v006a012
 | journal = [[Theory of Computing]]
 | mr = 2770077
 | pages = 291–308
 | title = Monotone expanders: constructions and applications
 | volume = 6
 | year = 2010| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

The edges within a single page of a book embedding behave in some ways like a [[Stack (abstract data type)|stack data structure]]. This can be formalized by considering an arbitrary sequence of push and pop operations on a stack, and forming a graph in which the stack operations correspond to the vertices of the graph, placed in sequence order along the spine of a book embedding. Then, if one draws an edge from each pop operation that pops an object {{mvar|x}} from the stack, to the previous push operation that pushed {{mvar|x}}, the resulting graph will automatically have a one-page embedding. For this reason, the page number of a graph has also been called its '''stack number'''. In the same way, one may consider an arbitrary sequence of enqueue and dequeue operations of a [[Queue (abstract data type)|queue data structure]], and form a graph that has these operations as its vertices, placed in order on the spine of a single page, with an edge between each enqueue operation and the corresponding dequeue. Then, in this graph, each two edges will either cross or cover disjoint intervals on the spine. By analogy, researchers have defined a queue embedding of a graph to be an embedding in a topological book such that each vertex lies on the spine, each edge lies in a single page, and each two edges in the same page either cross or cover disjoint intervals on the spine. The minimum number of pages needed for a queue embedding of a graph is called its [[queue number]].<ref name="nodm"/><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Heath | first1 = Lenwood S.
 | last2 = Rosenberg | first2 = Arnold L.
 | doi = 10.1137/0221055
 | issue = 5
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Computing]]
 | mr = 1181408
 | pages = 927–958
 | title = Laying out graphs using queues
 | volume = 21
 | year = 1992}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Dujmović | first1 = Vida | author1-link = Vida Dujmović
 | last2 = Wood | first2 = David R. | author2-link = David Wood (mathematician)
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Discrete Mathematics & Theoretical Computer Science
 | mr = 2081479
 | pages = 339–357
 | title = On linear layouts of graphs
 | volume = 6
 | year = 2004}}.</ref>

===Computational complexity===
[[File:Circle graph and circle model.svg|thumb|A [[circle graph]], the [[intersection graph]] of chords of a circle. For book embeddings with a fixed vertex order, finding the book thickness is equivalent to coloring a derived circle graph.|alt=Refer to caption]]
Finding the book thickness of a graph is [[NP-hard]]. This follows from the fact that finding Hamiltonian cycles in maximal planar graphs is [[NP-complete]].<ref>{{citation | url=https://www.math.ias.edu/avi/node/820 | title=The Complexity of the Hamiltonian Circuit Problem for Maximal Planar Graphs|first=Avi |last=Wigderson|author-link=Avi Wigderson|type=Technical Report #298|publisher=Department of EECS, Princeton University|date=February 1982|via=Institute for Advanced Study }}</ref> In a maximal planar graph, the book thickness is two if and only if a Hamiltonian cycle exists. Therefore, it is also NP-complete to test whether the book thickness of a given maximal planar graph is two.<ref name="clr"/>

If an ordering of the vertices of a graph along the spine of an embedding is fixed, then a two-page embedding (if it exists) can be found in [[linear time]], as an instance of [[planarity testing]] for a graph formed by augmenting the given graph with a cycle connecting the vertices in their spine ordering.<ref name="hs99"/> {{harvtxt|Unger|1992}} claimed that finding three-page embeddings with a fixed spine ordering can also be performed in [[polynomial time]] although his writeup of this result omits many details.<ref name="u-stacs-92">{{citation
 | last = Unger | first = Walter
 | contribution = The complexity of colouring circle graphs
 | doi = 10.1007/3-540-55210-3_199
 | location = Berlin
 | pages = 389–400
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = STACS 92: 9th Annual Symposium on Theoretical Aspects of Computer Science, Cachan, France, February 13–15, 1992, Proceedings
 | volume = 577
 | year = 1992| isbn = 978-3-540-55210-9
 }}.</ref> However, for graphs that require four or more pages, the problem of finding an embedding with the minimum possible number of pages remains NP-hard, via an equivalence to the NP-hard problem of [[Graph coloring|coloring]] [[circle graph]]s, the [[intersection graph]]s of [[Chord (geometry)|chords]] of a [[circle]]. Given a graph {{mvar|G}} with a fixed spine ordering for its vertices, drawing these vertices in the same order around a circle and drawing the edges of {{mvar|G}} as line segments produces a collection of chords representing {{mvar|G}}. One can then form a circle graph that has the chords of this diagram as vertices and crossing pairs of chords as edges. A coloring of the circle graph represents a partition of the edges of {{mvar|G}} into subsets that can be drawn without crossing on a single page. Therefore, an optimal coloring is equivalent to an optimal book embedding. Since circle graph coloring with four or more colors is NP-hard, and since any circle graph can be formed in this way from some book embedding problem, it follows that optimal book embedding is also NP-hard.<ref name="u88">{{citation
 | last = Unger | first = Walter
 | contribution = On the k-colouring of circle-graphs
 | doi = 10.1007/BFb0035832
 | pages = 61–72
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Proceedings of the 5th Symposium on Theoretical Aspects of Computer Science (STACS '88)
 | volume = 294
 | year = 1988| title-link = Symposium on Theoretical Aspects of Computer Science
 | isbn = 3-540-18834-7
 }}.</ref><ref name="mnkf">{{citation
 | last1 = Masuda | first1 = Sumio
 | last2 = Nakajima | first2 = Kazuo
 | last3 = Kashiwabara | first3 = Toshinobu
 | last4 = Fujisawa | first4 = Toshio
 | doi = 10.1109/12.46286
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[IEEE Transactions on Computers]]
 | mr = 1032144
 | pages = 124–127
 | title = Crossing minimization in linear embeddings of graphs
 | volume = 39
 | year = 1990
 | bibcode = 1990ITCmp..39..124M
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Garey | first1 = M. R. | author1-link = Michael Garey
 | last2 = Johnson | first2 = D. S. | author2-link = David S. Johnson
 | last3 = Miller | first3 = G. L. | author3-link = Gary Miller (computer scientist)
 | last4 = Papadimitriou | first4 = C. H. | author4-link = Christos Papadimitriou
 | doi = 10.1137/0601025
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods]]
 | mr = 578325
 | pages = 216–227
 | title = The complexity of coloring circular arcs and chords
 | volume = 1
 | year = 1980}}.</ref> For a fixed vertex ordering on the spine of a two-page book drawing, it is also NP-hard to minimize the number of crossings when this number is nonzero.<ref name="mnkf"/>

If the spine ordering is unknown but a partition of the edges into two pages is given, then it is possible to find a 2-page embedding (if it exists) in [[linear time]] by an algorithm based on [[SPQR tree]]s.<ref name="hn09">{{citation
 | last1 = Hong
 | first1 = Seok-Hee
 | author1-link = Seok-Hee Hong
 | last2 = Nagamochi
 | first2 = Hiroshi
 | edition = 2009-004
 | publisher = Dept. of Applied Mathematics and Physics, University of Kyoto, Japan
 | series = Technical report
 | title = Two-page book embedding and clustered graph planarity
 | url = http://www-or.amp.i.kyoto-u.ac.jp/members/nag/Technical_report/TR2009-004.pdf
 | year = 2009
 | access-date = 2014-06-16
 | archive-date = 2020-09-24
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200924051546/http://www-or.amp.i.kyoto-u.ac.jp/members/nag/Technical_report/TR2009-004.pdf
 | url-status = dead
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Angelini | first1 = Patrizio
 | last2 = Di Bartolomeo | first2 = Marco
 | last3 = Di Battista | first3 = Giuseppe
 | contribution = Implementing a partitioned 2-page book embedding testing algorithm
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-36763-2_8
 | mr = 3067219
 | pages = 79–89
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Graph Drawing: 20th International Symposium, GD 2012, Redmond, WA, USA, September 19–21, 2012, Revised Selected Papers
 | volume = 7704
 | year = 2013| arxiv = 1209.0598| title-link = International Symposium on Graph Drawing
 | isbn = 978-3-642-36762-5
 }}.</ref> However, it is NP-complete to find a 2-page embedding when neither the spine ordering nor the edge partition is known. Finding the book crossing number of a graph is also NP-hard, because of the NP-completeness of the special case of testing whether the 2-page crossing number is zero.

As a consequence of bounded expansion, the [[subgraph isomorphism]] problem, of finding whether a pattern graph of bounded size exists as a subgraph of a larger graph, can be solved in linear time when the larger graph has bounded book thickness. The same is true for detecting whether the pattern graph is an [[induced subgraph]] of the larger graph, or whether it has a [[graph homomorphism]] to the larger graph.<ref>{{harvtxt|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012}}, Corollary 18.1, p.&nbsp;401.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Nešetřil | first1 = Jaroslav | author1-link = Jaroslav Nešetřil
 | last2 = Ossona de Mendez | first2 = Patrice
 | doi = 10.1016/j.ejc.2006.07.014
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[European Journal of Combinatorics]]
 | mr = 2397336
 | pages = 777–791
 | title = Grad and classes with bounded expansion. II. Algorithmic aspects
 | volume = 29
 | year = 2008| arxiv = math/0508324}}.</ref> For the same reason, the problem of testing whether a graph of bounded book thickness obeys a given formula of [[first order logic]] is [[parameterized complexity|fixed-parameter tractable]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012}}, Theorem 18.7, p.&nbsp;405.</ref>

{{harvtxt|Bekos|Kaufmann|Zielke|2015}} describe a system for finding optimal book embeddings by transforming the problem into an instance of the [[Boolean satisfiability problem]] and applying a SAT solver to the resulting problem. They state that their system is capable of finding an optimal embedding for 400-vertex [[maximal planar graph]]s in approximately 20 minutes.<ref name="bkz15"/>

==Applications==

===Fault-tolerant multiprocessing===
One of the main motivations for studying book embedding cited by {{harvtxt|Chung|Leighton|Rosenberg|1987}} involves an application in [[VLSI]] design, to the organization of [[fault tolerance|fault-tolerant]] [[multiprocessor]]s. In the DIOGENES system developed by these authors, the [[CPU]]s of a multiprocessor system are arranged into a logical sequence corresponding to the spine of a book (although this sequence may not necessarily be placed along a line in the [[physical layout]] of this system). Communication links connecting these processors are grouped into "bundles" which correspond to the pages of a book and act like [[Stack (abstract data type)|stacks]]: connecting one of the processors to the start of a new communications link pushes all the previous links upward in the bundle, and connecting another processor to the end of a communication link connects it to the one at the bottom of the bundle and pops all the other ones down. Because of this stack behavior, a single bundle can handle a set of communications links that form the edges of a single page in a book embedding.  By organizing the links in this way, a wide variety of different network topologies can be implemented, regardless of which processors have become faulty, as long as enough non-faulty processors remain to implement the network.  The network topologies that can be implemented by this system are exactly the ones that have book thickness at most equal to the number of bundles that have been made available.<ref name="clr">{{citation
 | last1 = Chung | first1 = Fan R. K. | author1-link = Fan Chung
 | last2 = Leighton | first2 = Frank Thompson | author2-link = F. Thomson Leighton
 | last3 = Rosenberg | first3 = Arnold L. | author3-link = Arnold L. Rosenberg
 | doi = 10.1137/0608002
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods]]
 | pages = 33–58
 | title = Embedding graphs in books: A layout problem with applications to VLSI design
 | url = http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~fan/mypaps/fanpap/fc82embedding.pdf
 | volume = 8
 | year = 1987}}.</ref>
Book embedding may also be used to model the placement of wires connecting VLSI components into the layers of a circuit.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Rosenberg | first = Arnold L. | authorlink = Arnold L. Rosenberg
 | contribution = Book embeddings and wafer-scale integration
 | series = Congressus Numerantium
 | mr = 885282
 | pages = 217–224
 | title = Proceedings of the seventeenth Southeastern international conference on combinatorics, graph theory, and computing (Boca Raton, Fla., 1986)
 | volume = 54
 | year = 1986}}.</ref>

===Stack sorting===
Another application cited by {{harvtxt|Chung|Leighton|Rosenberg|1987}} concerns sorting [[permutation]]s using [[Stack (abstract data type)|stack]]s.
An influential result of {{harvs|first=Donald|last=Knuth|authorlink=Donald Knuth|year=1968|txt}} showed that a system that processes a [[data stream]] by pushing incoming elements onto a 
stack and then, at appropriately chosen times, popping them from the stack onto an output stream can [[sorting algorithm|sort]] the data if and only if its initial order is described by a [[permutation]] that avoids the [[permutation pattern]] 231.<ref>{{ Citation
 | last=Knuth
 | first=Donald E.
 | author-link=Donald Knuth
 | title=The Art Of Computer Programming Vol. 1
 | at = Section 2.2.1, Exercises 4 and 5
 | publisher=Addison-Wesley
 | place=Boston
 | year=1968
 | isbn=0-201-89683-4
 | oclc=155842391
 | mr= 0286317| title-link=The Art of Computer Programming
 }}.</ref> Since then, there has been much work on similar problems of sorting data streams by more general systems of stacks and queues. In the system considered by {{harvtxt|Chung|Leighton|Rosenberg|1987}}, each element from an input data stream must be pushed onto one of several stacks. Then, once all of the data has been pushed in this way, the items are popped from these stacks (in an appropriate order) onto an output stream. As Chung et al. observe, a given permutation can be sorted by this system if and only if a certain graph, derived from the permutation, has a book embedding with the vertices in a certain fixed order along the spine and with a number of pages that is at most equal to the number of stacks.<ref name="clr"/>

===Traffic control===
[[File:Street Intersection diagram.PNG|thumb|upright=1.5|A traffic intersection. The four incoming and four outgoing pairs of through lanes, two turn pockets, and four crosswalk corners can be represented as a set of 14 vertices on the spine of a book embedding, with edges representing connections between these points.|alt=Refer to caption]]
As {{harvtxt|Kainen|1990}} described, a book embedding may be used to describe the phases of a [[traffic signal]] at a controlled intersection.
At an intersection, the incoming and outgoing lanes of traffic (including the ends of pedestrian crosswalks and bicycle lanes as well as lanes for motor vehicles) may be represented as the vertices of a graph, placed on the spine of a book embedding in their clockwise order around the junction. The paths through the intersection taken by traffic to get from an incoming lane to an outgoing lane may be represented as the edges of an undirected graph. For instance, this graph might have an edge from an incoming to an outgoing lane of traffic that both belong to the same segment of road, representing a U-turn from that segment back to that segment, only if U-turns are allowed at the junction. For a given subset of these edges, the subset represents a collection of paths that can all be traversed without interference from each other if and only if the subset does not include any pair of edges that would cross if the two edges were placed in a single page of a book embedding. Thus, a book embedding of this graph describes a partition of the paths into non-interfering subsets, and the book thickness of this graph (with its fixed embedding on the spine) gives the minimum number of distinct phases needed for a signalling schedule that includes all possible traffic paths through the junction.<ref name="kainen">{{citation
 | last = Kainen | first = Paul C. | author-link = Paul Chester Kainen
 | contribution = The book thickness of a graph. II
 | mr = 1041623
 | pages = 127–132
 | series = Congressus Numerantium
 | title = Proceedings of the Twentieth Southeastern Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory, and Computing (Boca Raton, FL, 1989)
 | volume = 71
 | year = 1990}}.</ref>

===Graph drawing===
[[File:Goldner-Harary-linear.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|An [[arc diagram]] of the [[Goldner–Harary graph]]. In order to create a planar diagram, two triangles of the graph have been subdivided into four by the dashed red line, causing one of the graph edges to extend both above and below the line.|alt=Refer to caption]]
Book embedding has also been frequently applied in the visualization of network data. Two of the standard layouts in [[graph drawing]], arc diagrams<ref name="w02"/> and circular layouts,<ref name="bb"/> can be viewed as book embeddings, and book embedding has also been applied in the construction of clustered layouts,<ref name="hn09"/> simultaneous embeddings,<ref name="adfpr"/> and three-dimensional graph drawings.<ref name="wood02"/>

An [[arc diagram]]<ref name="w02">{{citation
 | last = Wattenberg | first = M. | authorlink = Martin M. Wattenberg
 | contribution = Arc diagrams: visualizing structure in strings
 | doi = 10.1109/INFVIS.2002.1173155
 | pages = 110–116
 | title = Proceedings of IEEE Symposium on Information Visualization (INFOVIS 2002)
 | year = 2002| isbn = 0-7695-1751-X}}.</ref> or linear embedding<ref name="mnkf"/> places vertices of a graph along a line, and draws the edges of the graph as semicircles either above or below this line, sometimes also allowing edges to be drawn on segments of the line. This drawing style corresponds to a book embedding with either one page (if all semicircles are above the line) or two pages (if both sides of the line are used), and was originally introduced as a way of studying the [[Crossing number (graph theory)|crossing numbers]] of graphs.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Saaty | first = Thomas L. | authorlink = Thomas L. Saaty
 | journal = [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]
 | mr = 0166772
 | pages = 688–690
 | title = The minimum number of intersections in complete graphs
 | volume = 52
 | issue = 3 | year = 1964
 | doi=10.1073/pnas.52.3.688| pmc = 300329| bibcode = 1964PNAS...52..688S | pmid=16591215| doi-access = free }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Nicholson | first = T. A. J.
 | doi = 10.1049/piee.1968.0004
 | journal = Proceedings of the Institution of Electrical Engineers
 | mr = 0311416
 | pages = 21–26
 | title = Permutation procedure for minimising the number of crossings in a network
 | volume = 115
 | year = 1968}}.</ref> Planar graphs that do not have two-page book embeddings may also be drawn in a similar way, by allowing their edges to be represented by multiple semicircles above and below the line. Such a drawing is not a book embedding by the usual definition, but has been called a '''topological book embedding'''.<ref>{{citation|first=Miki|last=Miyauchi|title=Topological book embedding of bipartite graphs|journal=IEICE Transactions on Fundamentals of Electronics, Communications and Computer Sciences|year=2006|volume=E89-A|issue=5|pages=1223–1226|doi=10.1093/ietfec/e89-a.5.1223|bibcode=2006IEITF..89.1223M}}.</ref> For every planar graph, it is always possible to find such an embedding in which each edge crosses the spine at most once.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Giordano | first1 = Francesco
 | last2 = Liotta | first2 = Giuseppe
 | last3 = Mchedlidze | first3 = Tamara
 | last4 = Symvonis | first4 = Antonios
 | contribution = Computing upward topological book embeddings of upward planar digraphs
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-77120-3_17
 | pages = 172–183
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Algorithms and Computation: 18th International Symposium, ISAAC 2007, Sendai, Japan, December 17–19, 2007, Proceedings
 | volume = 4835
 | year = 2007| title-link = International Symposium on Algorithms and Computation
 | isbn = 978-3-540-77118-0
 | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

[[File:Chvatal Lombardi.svg|thumb|Circular layout of the [[Chvátal graph]]|alt=Refer to caption]]
In another drawing style, the [[circular layout]], the vertices of a graph are placed on a circle and the edges are drawn either inside or outside the circle.<ref name="bb">{{citation
 | last1 = Baur | first1 = Michael
 | last2 = Brandes | first2 = Ulrik | author2-link = Ulrik Brandes
 | editor-last = van Leeuwen | editor-first = Jan
 | contribution = Crossing reduction in circular layouts
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-30559-0_28
 | pages = 332–343
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Graph-Theoretic Concepts in Computer Science: 30th International Workshop, WG 2004, Bad Honnef, Germany, June 21-23, 2004, Revised Papers
 | volume = 3353
 | year = 2005| isbn = 978-3-540-24132-4
 | url = https://publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu/1000001244/1027
 | url-access = subscription
 }}.</ref> Again, a placement of the edges within the circle (for instance as straight line segments) corresponds to a one-page book drawing, while a placement both inside and outside the circle corresponds to a two-page book drawing.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = He | first1 = Hongmei
 | last2 = Sykora | first2 = Ondrej
 | contribution = New circular drawing algorithms
 | title = Proceedings of the Workshop on Information Technologies – Applications and Theory (ITAT), Slovakia, September 15–19, 2004
 | url = https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/2134/2386
 | year = 2004}}.</ref>

For one-page drawings of either style, it is important to keep the number of crossings small as a way of reducing the visual clutter of the drawing. Minimizing the number of crossings is [[NP-complete]],<ref name="mnkf"/> but may be approximated with an approximation ratio of {{math|''O''(log<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;''n'')}} where {{mvar|n}} is the number of vertices.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Shahrokhi | first1 = Farhad
 | last2 = Sýkora | first2 = Ondrej
 | last3 = Székely | first3 = László A.
 | last4 = Vrt'o | first4 = Imrich
 | contribution = Book embeddings and crossing numbers
 | doi = 10.1007/3-540-59071-4_53
 | pages = 256–268
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Graph-Theoretic Concepts in Computer Science: 20th International Workshop, WG '94, Herrsching, Germany, June 16–18, 1994, Proceedings
 | volume = 903
 | year = 1995| isbn = 978-3-540-59071-2
 }}.</ref> Minimizing the one-page or two-page crossing number is [[fixed-parameter tractable]] when parameterized by the [[cyclomatic number]] of the given graph, or by a combination of the crossing number and the [[treewidth]] of the graph.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Bannister | first1 = Michael J.
 | last2 = Eppstein | first2 = David | author2-link = David Eppstein
 | last3 = Simons | first3 = Joseph A.
 | arxiv = 1308.5741
 | contribution = Fixed parameter tractability of crossing minimization of almost-trees
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-03841-4_30
 | pages = 340–351
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Graph Drawing: 21st International Symposium, GD 2013, Bordeaux, France, September 23–25, 2013, Revised Selected Papers
 | volume = 8242
 | year = 2013| title-link = International Symposium on Graph Drawing
 | isbn = 978-3-319-03840-7
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Bannister | first1 = Michael J.
 | last2 = Eppstein | first2 = David | author2-link = David Eppstein
 | arxiv = 1408.6321
 | contribution = Crossing minimization for 1-page and 2-page drawings of graphs with bounded treewidth
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-662-45803-7_18
 | mr = 3333228
 | pages = 210–221
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Proc. 22nd Int. Symp. Graph Drawing (GD 2014)
 | volume = 8871
 | year = 2014| isbn = 978-3-319-12567-1
 }}.</ref> Heuristic methods for reducing the crossing complexity have also been devised, based e.g. on a careful vertex insertion order and on [[Local search (optimization)|local optimization]].<ref name="bb"/>

Two-page book embeddings with a fixed partition of the edges into pages can be interpreted as a form of [[clustered planarity]], in which the given graph must be drawn in such a way that parts of the graph (the two subsets of edges) are placed in the drawing in a way that reflects their clustering.<ref name="hn09"/> Two-page book embedding has also been used to find [[simultaneous embedding]]s of graphs, in which two graphs are given on the same vertex set and one must find a placement for the vertices in which both graphs are drawn planarly with straight edges.<ref name="adfpr">{{citation
 | last1 = Angelini | first1 = Patrizio
 | last2 = Di Battista | first2 = Giuseppe
 | last3 = Frati | first3 = Fabrizio
 | last4 = Patrignani | first4 = Maurizio
 | last5 = Rutter | first5 = Ignaz
 | doi = 10.1016/j.jda.2011.12.015
 | journal = Journal of Discrete Algorithms
 | mr = 2922068
 | pages = 150–172
 | title = Testing the simultaneous embeddability of two graphs whose intersection is a biconnected or a connected graph
 | volume = 14
 | year = 2012| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

Book embeddings with more than two pages have also been used to construct three-dimensional drawings of graphs. In particular, {{harvtxt|Wood|2002}} used a construction for book embeddings that keep the [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] of each vertex within each page low, as part of a method for embedding graphs into a three-dimensional grid of low volume.<ref name="wood02">{{citation
 | last = Wood | first = David R. | authorlink=David Wood (mathematician)
 | contribution = Bounded degree book embeddings and three-dimensional orthogonal graph drawing
 | doi = 10.1007/3-540-45848-4_25
 | mr = 1962433
 | pages = 312–327
 | publisher = Springer, Berlin
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Graph Drawing: 9th International Symposium, GD 2001, Vienna, Austria, September 23–26, 2001, Revised Papers
 | volume = 2265
 | year = 2002| title-link = International Symposium on Graph Drawing
 | doi-access = free
 | isbn = 978-3-540-43309-5 }}.</ref>

===RNA folding===
[[File:Pseudoknot.svg|upright=1.5|thumb|A fragment of human [[telomerase]] showing a [[pseudoknot]]. If the fragment is stretched straight along the spine of a book embedding, the blue base pairs can be drawn in two non-crossing subsets above and below the spine, showing that this pseudoknot forms a bi-secondary structure.|alt=Refer to caption]]
In the study of how [[RNA]] molecules fold to form their structure, the standard form of [[nucleic acid secondary structure]] can be described diagrammatically as a chain of bases (the RNA sequence itself), drawn along a line, together with a collection of arcs above the line describing the [[basepair]]s of the structure. That is, although these structures actually have a complicated three-dimensional shape, their connectivity (when a secondary structure exists) can be described by a more abstract structure, a one-page book embedding. However, not all RNA folds behave in this simple way. {{harvtxt|Haslinger|Stadler|1999}} have proposed a so-called "bi-secondary structure" for certain RNA [[pseudoknot]]s that takes the form of a two-page book embedding: the RNA sequence is again drawn along a line, but the basepairs are drawn as arcs both above and below this line. In order to form a bi-secondary structure, a graph must have maximum degree at most three: each base can only participate in one arc of the diagram, in addition to the two links to its neighbors in the base sequence. Advantages of this formulation include the facts that it excludes structures that are actually knotted in space, and that it matches most known RNA pseudoknots.<ref name="hs99">{{citation
 | last1 = Haslinger | first1 = Christian
 | last2 = Stadler | first2 = Peter F.
 | doi = 10.1006/bulm.1998.0085
 | pmid = 17883226
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Bulletin of Mathematical Biology]]
 | pages = 437–467
 | title = RNA structures with pseudo-knots: Graph-theoretical, combinatorial, and statistical properties
 | volume = 61
 | year = 1999| pmc = 7197269
 }}.</ref>

Because the spine ordering is known in advance for this application, testing for the existence of a bi-secondary structure for a given basepairing is straightforward. The problem of assigning edges to the two pages in a compatible way can be formulated as either an instance of [[2-satisfiability]], or as a problem of testing the [[bipartite graph|bipartiteness]] of the [[circle graph]] whose vertices are the basepairs and whose edges describe crossings between basepairs.<ref name="hs99"/> Alternatively and more efficiently, as  {{harvtxt|Haslinger|Stadler|1999}} show, a bi-secondary structure exists if and only if the ''diagram graph'' of the input (a graph formed by connecting the bases into a cycle in their sequence order and adding the given basepairs as edges) is a [[planar graph]].<ref name="hs99"/> This characterization allows bi-secondary structures to be recognized in [[linear time]] as an instance of [[planarity testing]].

{{harvtxt|Blin|Fertin|Rusu|Sinoquet|2007}} used the connection between secondary structures and book embeddings as part of a proof of the [[NP-hard]]ness of certain problems in RNA secondary structure comparison.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Blin | first1 = Guillaume
 | last2 = Fertin | first2 = Guillaume
 | last3 = Rusu | first3 = Irena
 | last4 = Sinoquet | first4 = Christine
 | contribution = Extending the hardness of RNA secondary structure comparison
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-74450-4_13
 | pages = 140–151
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Combinatorics, Algorithms, Probabilistic and Experimental Methodologies: First International Symposium, ESCAPE 2007, Hangzhou, China, April 7-9, 2007, Revised Selected Papers
 | volume = 4614
 | year = 2007| isbn = 978-3-540-74449-8
 | url = https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00418248/file/ESCAPE07.pdf
 }}.</ref> And if an RNA structure is tertiary rather than bi-secondary (that is, if it requires more than two pages in its diagram), then determining the page number is again NP-hard.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Clote | first1 = Peter
 | last2 = Dobrev | first2 = Stefan
 | last3 = Dotu | first3 = Ivan
 | last4 = Kranakis | first4 = Evangelos
 | last5 = Krizanc | first5 = Danny
 | last6 = Urrutia | first6 = Jorge | author6-link = Jorge Urrutia Galicia
 | doi = 10.1007/s00285-011-0493-6
 | pmid = 22159642
 | issue = 6–7
 | journal = [[Journal of Mathematical Biology]]
 | pages = 1337–1357
 | title = On the page number of RNA secondary structures with pseudoknots
 | volume = 65
 | year = 2012
 }}.</ref>

===Computational complexity theory===
{{harvtxt|Pavan|Tewari|Vinodchandran|2012}} used book embedding to study the [[computational complexity theory]] of the [[reachability]] problem in [[directed graph]]s. As they have observed, reachability for two-page directed graphs may be solved in unambiguous logarithmic space (the analogue, for [[L (complexity)|logarithmic space complexity]], of the class [[UP (complexity)|UP]] of unambiguous polynomial-time problems). However, reachability for three-page directed graphs requires the full power of [[NL (complexity)|nondeterministic logarithmic space]]. Thus, book embeddings seem intimately connected with the distinction between these two complexity classes.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Pavan | first1 = A.
 | last2 = Tewari | first2 = Raghunath
 | last3 = Vinodchandran | first3 = N. V.
 | doi = 10.1007/s00037-012-0047-3
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Computational Complexity
 | mr = 2988774
 | pages = 643–670
 | title = On the power of unambiguity in log-space
 | volume = 21
 | year = 2012| arxiv = 1001.2034
 }}.</ref>

The existence of [[expander graph]]s with constant page number<ref name="dsw15"/> is the key step in proving that there is no subquadratic-time simulation of two-tape [[non-deterministic Turing machine]]s by one-tape non-deterministic Turing machines.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Galil | first1 = Zvi | author1-link = Zvi Galil
 | last2 = Kannan | first2 = Ravi | author2-link = Ravindran Kannan
 | last3 = Szemerédi | first3 = Endre | author3-link = Endre Szemerédi
 | doi = 10.1016/0022-0000(89)90036-6
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Journal of Computer and System Sciences]]
 | pages = 134–149
 | title = On nontrivial separators for k-page graphs and simulations by nondeterministic one-tape Turing machines
 | volume = 38
 | year = 1989| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

===Other areas of mathematics===
{{harvtxt|McKenzie|Overbay|2010}} study applications of book thickness in [[abstract algebra]], using graphs defined from the [[zero divisor]]s of a finite [[local ring]] by making a vertex for each zero divisor and an edge for each pair of values whose product is zero.<ref name="mo10">{{citation
 | last1 = McKenzie | first1 = Thomas
 | last2 = Overbay | first2 = Shannon
 | journal = [[Ars Combinatoria (journal)|Ars Combinatoria]]
 | mr = 2656248
 | pages = 55–63
 | title = Book embeddings and zero divisors
 | volume = 95
 | year = 2010}}.</ref>

In a multi-paper sequence, Dynnikov has studied the topological book embeddings of [[knot (mathematics)|knots]] and [[Link (knot theory)|links]], showing that these embeddings can be described by a combinatorial sequence of symbols and that the topological equivalence of two links can be demonstrated by a sequence of local changes to the embeddings.<ref name="dyn99">{{citation
 | last = Dynnikov | first = I. A.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02467109
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Rossiĭskaya Akademiya Nauk
 | mr = 1746427
 | pages = 25–37, 96
 | title = Three-page approach to knot theory. Coding and local motions
 | volume = 33
 | year = 1999
 }}.</ref><ref name="dyn01">{{citation
 | last = Dynnikov | first = I. A.
 | doi = 10.1023/A:1014299416618
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Acta Applicandae Mathematicae
 | mr = 1885279
 | pages = 243–283
 | title = A new way to represent links, one-dimensional formalism and untangling technology
 | volume = 69
 | year = 2001
 }}.</ref>
